subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Vaccination Nudges
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Vaccination Nudges.

hook.text: A clinic sent patients a text: your flu shot is reserved for Tuesday at 3pm.

buildup.text: Implementation intentions work: specifying when, where, and how increases follow-through.

discovery.text: Milkman showed pre-scheduled appointments and micro-incentives markedly boost vaccination rates more than information.

twist.text: Lottery incentives backfired in some vaccine drives. Paying people signaled the vaccine might be risky, reducing trust.

climax.text: The best vaccination nudge removes friction: close location, easy scheduling, and a specific time.

punchline.text: A scheduled appointment beats a thousand health reminders.

quiz.question: Why did specific appointment texts boost vaccination more than general reminders?
options: Implementation intentions with specific plans increase follow-through
Text messages are always more effective than other media

details.summary: Vaccination nudges use defaults, reminders, social norms, and implementation intentions to increase immunization rates. Simple interventions like scheduling a specific appointment time or sending personalized reminders can boost vaccination rates by 5 to 15 percent.
details.whyItMatters: Vaccination is one of public health's most effective tools, but uptake consistently falls short of targets. Behavioral nudges close the intention-action gap by making vaccination easy, timely, and socially normative rather than relying on.
takeaways: Pre-scheduled appointments dramatically increase vaccination attendance
Personalized reminders with specific dates are more effective than generic ones
Social norms messaging reduces vaccine hesitancy among fence-sitters

faq.question: What is the most effective nudge for increasing vaccination?
faq.answer: Pre-scheduled default appointments that people must actively cancel. This converts the action from opt-in to opt-out. Combined with reminders mentioning that a specific slot is reserved, attendance increases by 11 to 20 percent.

faq.question: Can nudges address vaccine hesitancy?
faq.answer: For fence-sitters, yes. Social norms messaging, trusted messenger effects, and reducing access friction help those who are uncertain. For strongly opposed individuals, nudges are insufficient and more intensive engagement is needed.
